title: What they share
hookLine: Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story
last: THESE AND THESE: NO STREAM SPEAKS FOR ALL.

cards: A long table on a spring night. One cousin wears a black hat. Another drove in from a congregation with a different prayer book.
A third hasn't been inside a synagogue in years. Someone at the far end has a kippah that keeps sliding off.
Then the youngest child stands and asks the question the seder sets for the youngest: why is this night different from all other nights?
And every head turns toward the same answer, the same story of slaves who walked out of Egypt. The streams run in different channels. Today is about the water they carry together.

teach.b: What they share. Five things, one for each finger. First, Torah.

The streams read the same five books, and hear the same line at their heart: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." They argue about how the Torah came to be and how to live it; that's tomorrow.
But the scroll in the ark is the same scroll. Second, Shabbat. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."
One family keeps every detail of the law. Another lights candles and turns off the phones for dinner. It's still the seventh day, and it still begins at sundown on Friday.

Third, the festivals. "These are the feasts of the LORD," Leviticus says, and it lists them: Passover, the counting to Shavuot, the new year, the Day of Atonement, Sukkot. Different prayer books, same calendar.
Fourth, the people. When Ruth joins her mother-in-law, she doesn't only say your God.

She says "thy people shall be my people" first. In her line, belonging to a family comes before the creed. Fifth, the story: Abraham and Sarah, the slavery, the sea, Sinai, the land, the exile, the long road home.
The streams tell it in different keys, and each tells it as its own.

A Hebrew phrase holds all of this: klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel. Not one movement; all of them. Psalm 133 says: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!"
Unity, there, doesn't mean sameness. It means sitting at one table.

how: Jews from different movements read the same Torah, keep the same weekly Shabbat and yearly festivals, and often speak of klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel, across their differences.

practice: Hold up one hand, fingers open, and fold one finger on each breath: Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people, the story.
Then open your hand and go around once more, slower, picturing for each finger one face you know, Jewish or not, who has something to do with it: a neighbor's candles, a friend's seder.

wordCard.voice: What they share. Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story: five things the streams of Judaism hold, even when they hold them differently. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the whole community of Israel, every Jew across every stream.
